steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by defining a component called App. For now, just have it return null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an App component defined that returns null.
successCriteria: The code should define a component named App (either as a function or arrow function) that returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component. Returning null for now is fine—we'll add content in later steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named App that returns null. Check your syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Ensure you create a component named App that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize state for the current value
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'value' with an initial value of 0.
steps.hint: Use useState<number>(0) to create a number state variable named value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a state variable 'value' initialized to 0 that can be used to track the current value.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with the variable name 'value' and initial value 0 inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the 'value' state variable with an initial value of 0. This will be the foundation for tracking the current value in our undo/redo system.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure you're using useState<number>(0) with the exact variable name 'value' inside the App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization doesn't match what's needed. Remember to use useState<number>(0) with the variable name 'value' inside the App component function body.

steps.title: Initialize state for the undo stack
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'past' with an initial value of an empty array ([]).
steps.hint: You'll need to call useState with [] as the initial value and destructure the array to get the state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing an array state
const [items, setItems] = useState<string[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a 'past' state variable initialized as an empty array, ready to store previous values for undo functionality.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call that creates a state variable named 'past' with an initial value of [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the 'past' state variable to track previous values for undo operations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've named the state variable exactly 'past' and initialized it with an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'past' state variable wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use useState with [] as the initial value.

steps.title: Initialize state for the redo stack
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'future' with an initial value of an empty array ([]).
steps.hint: Add a new useState call similar to the previous state variables, but name it 'future' and initialize it with [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable for a stack
const [future, setFuture] = useState<number[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a third state variable called 'future' that will store values for redo operations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the 'future' state variable. This will be used to track values that can be redone.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'future' with an initial value of an empty array.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires initializing a state variable named 'future' with an empty array using useState. Check your syntax and variable name.

steps.title: Define the handleIncrement function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleIncrement inside your App component. This function should increase the current value by 1 and update the undo stack.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates the current state and pushes the previous value to the past array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleIncrement function is defined and ready to be used to increment the current value while managing the undo stack.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named handleIncrement that updates the current state and pushes the previous current value to the past array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleIncrement function that updates the current value and manages the undo stack.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function updates both the current value and the past array. Check that you're using the setCurrent and setPast functions correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleIncrement function isn't defined correctly. Make sure you create a function that increases the current value by 1 and adds the previous value to the past array.

steps.title: Define the handleDecrement function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleDecrement that decreases the current value by 1 and updates the undo stack. The function should save the current value to the past array before updating current.
steps.hint: Inside the App component, create a function that uses setPast and setCurrent. Remember to update past with the current value before changing current.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleDecrement function is added to the component that properly updates both the past state and current state.
successCriteria: Function updates past state with current value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleDecrement function that properly manages the undo stack by saving the current value before decrementing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if your function: 1) is named handleDecrement, 2) saves current to past before updating current, and 3) decreases current by 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleDecrement function is not properly defined. Make sure to create a function that saves the current value to the past array and then decreases current by 1.

steps.title: Define the handleUndo function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleUndo inside your component. This function should move the last value from the past stack to current and update the future stack appropriately.
steps.hint: Check if there are any past values to undo. If there are, pop the last value from past, set it as current, and push the previous current value to future.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleUndo function that correctly manages the undo operation by moving values between the past, current, and future stacks.
successCriteria: The function must be named handleUndo, check if past has values, update past, future, and current states appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleUndo function. This function will allow users to revert to previous states.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your logic. Make sure you're correctly popping from past, updating future with the current value, and setting the new current.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleUndo function isn't defined correctly. Review the example and ensure you're moving values between the three state variables properly.

steps.title: Define the handleRedo function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleRedo inside your App component. This function should implement the redo logic: if there are any values in the future stack, move the last one to current, update past to include the previous current value, and clear that value from future.
steps.hint: Check if future has length > 0. If it does, pop the last value from future, set current to that value, and add the previous current value to past.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleRedo function that correctly implements the redo operation using the current, past, and future state variables.
successCriteria: The function must be named handleRedo, check if future has values, update current with the last future value, add the previous current to past, and remove that value from future.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your handleRedo function correctly implements the redo logic by moving values between the future and past stacks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a handleRedo function, but it might be missing some logic. Make sure it checks if future has values, updates all three state variables (current, past, future) correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleRedo function is not defined correctly. Ensure you create a function named handleRedo that implements the redo operation using the existing state variables.

steps.title: Add the current value display
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your App component, add a paragraph element that displays the current value from the 'current' state variable.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax with curly braces to embed the 'current' variable value in the paragraph text.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of displaying a state value in a paragraph

Current count: {count}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current numeric value (initially 0) below the heading.
successCriteria:
The code should include a

element that renders the 'current' state variable value using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the current value. This makes the state visible to the user.
steps.feedbackPartial:
You're close! Make sure you're using a

element and embedding the 'current' variable with curly braces like {current}.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph element displaying the current value is missing or incorrect. Remember to use

{current}

inside the return statement.

steps.title: Add increment and decrement buttons with click handlers
steps.instruction: Add two button elements inside the return statement: one with text 'Increment' that calls handleIncrement when clicked, and another with text 'Decrement' that calls handleDecrement when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick handlers. Place them after the paragraph element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will have two buttons: 'Increment' and 'Decrement'. Clicking them will modify the current value when the handlers are defined in later steps.
successCriteria: First button has text 'Increment' and onClick={handleIncrement}
Second button has text 'Decrement' and onClick={handleDecrement}
Buttons are placed after the paragraph element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the increment and decrement buttons with their click handlers. The UI now has interactive controls to modify the value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but check: Are there exactly two buttons? Do they have the correct text ('Increment' and 'Decrement')? Are the onClick handlers correctly set to handleIncrement and handleDecrement?
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or incorrect. You need to add two <button> elements with onClick handlers. The first should call handleIncrement and display 'Increment', the second should call handleDecrement and display 'Decrement'.

steps.title: Add undo and redo buttons with click handlers
steps.instruction: Add two button elements inside the return statement: one for undo with text 'Undo' and onClick set to handleUndo, and one for redo with text 'Redo' and onClick set to handleRedo.
steps.hint: Place the buttons after the increment/decrement buttons. Use the <button> tag with onClick={handleUndo} and onClick={handleRedo}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will have two new buttons labeled 'Undo' and 'Redo' that trigger the undo and redo functionality when clicked.
successCriteria: The code must include two <button> elements with onClick handlers set to handleUndo and handleRedo, and the buttons must have the text 'Undo' and 'Redo'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the undo and redo buttons with their click handlers. The UI now has all the interactive controls needed for the undo/redo functionality.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but make sure you have exactly two buttons: one with onClick={handleUndo} and text 'Undo', and another with onClick={handleRedo} and text 'Redo'. Check that both are present and correctly wired.
steps.feedbackWrong: The undo and redo buttons are missing or incorrectly implemented. You need to add two <button> elements with onClick handlers set to handleUndo and handleRedo, and label them 'Undo' and 'Redo'.
